forces.title: RBI consolidates tech regulations, creates new compliance framework.
forces.description: The Reserve Bank of India (RBI) issued Master Directions on July 31, 2026, consolidating regulatory expectations across regulated entities. This new entity-centric framework explicitly addresses cybersecurity and digital payments security, replacing fragmented instructions. Institutions are now required to align existing controls and governance structures immediately, signifying a major structural shift in the regulatory landscape for cybersecurity and digital payment security in India's financial sector.
forces.source_title: RBI’s technology focused master directions issued on 31 July 2026

forces.title: AI adoption introduces novel risks, intensifying cyber warfare.
forces.description: The rapid proliferation of Artificial Intelligence (AI) and other advanced technologies, including Operational Technology (OT), is creating novel risks and contributing to an environment of intense global cyber-warfare. This fuels relentless, sophisticated, and targeted cybersecurity attacks, demanding that organizations adapt their digital risk management strategies. The emergence of AI not only amplifies existing threats but also introduces entirely new attack vectors, making cybersecurity a boardroom priority.
forces.source_title: Secure in India 2026: Cyber GCCs in the age of AI

forces.title: RBI mandates comprehensive cybersecurity framework, 6-hour incident reporting.
forces.description: The RBI issued "Cybersecurity, Technology: Risk, Resilience and Assurance Framework Directions" on July 31, 2026, creating a unified regulatory framework for regulated entities. This includes detailed requirements for IT governance, 31 baseline control domains, operational resilience (BCP, DR, incident response), continuous monitoring, and explicit coverage of third-party risk. A significant change is the standalone Cyber Security Operations Centre chapter and a strict 6-hour incident reporting obligation to the DAKSH platform, increasing compliance burden and necessitating robust internal capabilities.
forces.source_title: RBI’s technology focused master directions issued on 31 July 2026

forces.title: Enhanced regulatory scrutiny on third-party cybersecurity risk.
forces.description: The RBI's new Cybersecurity Directions dedicate its longest sub-section within the baseline requirements to "Third party risk," covering arrangements not within the scope of outsourcing directions. This highlights a significant increase in regulatory focus on the cybersecurity posture of third-party vendors and partners. Regulated entities must ensure robust oversight and controls over all technology arrangements involving external parties, as these are now viewed as integral to their own cybersecurity resilience and subject to stringent compliance and assurance requirements.
forces.source_title: RBI’s technology focused master directions issued on 31 July 2026

forces.title: Cyber resilience elevated to boardroom priority, driving investments.
forces.description: The growing concentration of intellectual property, sensitive data, digital assets, and AI-driven systems, coupled with globally interconnected operations, has elevated cyber resilience to a boardroom priority. This strategic shift is driving enterprises, particularly through their Global Capability Centers (GCCs), to significantly invest in advanced threat detection, cloud security, AI-enabled security operations, identity-centric architectures, and third-party risk management. The imperative is to establish trust, secure digital operations, and maintain stakeholder confidence in a rapidly evolving threat environment.
forces.source_title: Secure in India 2026: Cyber GCCs in the age of AI

forces.title: RBI strengthens digital payment security with comprehensive controls.
forces.description: The RBI's "Digital Payment Security Controls Directions," issued July 31, 2026, establish a comprehensive security framework for digital payment channels and transactions. Applicable to five regulated entities, it mandates board-approved policies for digital payment products, detailed channel-specific architectures, robust authentication frameworks, and enhanced fraud risk management and reconciliation mechanisms. This applies to both financial and non-financial transactions, significantly raising the bar for cybersecurity in the digital payments ecosystem and increasing demand for related security solutions.
forces.source_title: RBI’s technology focused master directions issued on 31 July 2026

forces.title: Weaponization of cybersecurity and AI-driven attacks escalate threat landscape.
forces.description: The global business landscape is increasingly facing the weaponization of cybersecurity, with cybercriminals leveraging AI to sharpen their methods, create convincing phishing campaigns, and launch identity-driven attacks. This dynamic creates a double challenge: managing external AI risks while ensuring internal AI tools are secure, transparent, and well-governed. This escalating threat environment necessitates a re-evaluation of cybersecurity strategies, as traditional defenses may be insufficient against rapidly evolving, AI-powered adversarial techniques, driving demand for advanced security solutions.
forces.source_title: Secure in India 2026: Cyber GCCs in the age of AI

forces.title: "Make in India" cybersecurity products diversify trusted supply chains.
forces.description: India is actively building a sustainable cybersecurity ecosystem by fostering innovation and developing indigenous capabilities, creating opportunities to integrate and scale "Make in India" cybersecurity products. This initiative is a significant upside driver for the cybersecurity sector, as it helps diversify trusted supply chains for global organizations. By offering locally developed solutions, it enhances resilience against geopolitical risks and supply chain disruptions, reducing reliance on foreign vendors and potentially creating new market opportunities for domestic cybersecurity firms.
forces.source_title: Secure in India 2026: Cyber GCCs in the age of AI

forces.title: India's cyber GCCs attract significant global cybersecurity workforce.
forces.description: Over 25% of cyber Global Capability Centers (GCCs) in India now host nearly 50% of their global cybersecurity workforce, with 22% operating large teams exceeding 100 professionals. This expansion, driven by the availability of skilled resources, uninterrupted service delivery, and continuous innovation, highlights India's growing importance as a talent hub. The increasing role and influence of cyber GCCs, with global teams reporting to India-based leadership and representation in international committees, acts as a strong tailwind for the cybersecurity sector in India.
forces.source_title: Secure in India 2026: Cyber GCCs in the age of AI

forces.title: AI security emerges as critical cybersecurity function in GCCs.
forces.description: AI security is rapidly emerging as a key cybersecurity function within cyber Global Capability Centers (GCCs), joining established areas like cybersecurity risk assessments, operations, Third-Party Risk Management (TPRM), and Identity and Access Management (IAM). This shift reflects the necessity to secure AI systems and leverage AI for enhanced defenses. The integration of AI security into core functions signifies a structural change in cybersecurity priorities, driving demand for specialized skills and solutions tailored to managing AI-induced threats and vulnerabilities.
forces.source_title: Secure in India 2026: Cyber GCCs in the age of AI

forces.title: RBI mandates stringent cyber incident reporting and testing.
forces.description: New RBI directions impose a strict six-hour cyber incident reporting obligation to the DAKSH platform, coupled with proactive notification to CERT-In. Additionally, critical information systems require vulnerability assessments at least semi-annually and penetration testing annually. Disaster recovery drills for critical systems are also mandated half-yearly with re-test requirements. These stringent compliance mandates significantly increase the operational burden and demand for continuous security monitoring, rapid incident response capabilities, and regular security assurance services within regulated entities.
forces.source_title: RBI’s technology focused master directions issued on 31 July 2026

forces.title: AI security skills top priority, boosting cybersecurity talent demand.
forces.description: AI security, encompassing "AI for security" and "security of AI," is identified as a top priority skillset for cyber Global Capability Centers (GCCs). This specialized demand is sharply increasing for cybersecurity talent in strategic areas such as governance, resilience, AI security, risk assessments, architecture, and cloud security. The focus on AI-driven cybersecurity is reshaping the talent landscape, requiring continuous upskilling and new learning ecosystems. While GCCs benefit from low attrition due to career mobility and AI-powered security, competitive compensation remains a challenge.
forces.source_title: Secure in India 2026: Cyber GCCs in the age of AI

forces.title: AI acts as force multiplier for cybersecurity defense efficiency.
forces.description: Artificial Intelligence (AI) is proving to be a force multiplier for cyber Global Capability Centers (GCCs), significantly enhancing operational efficiency, risk and threat management, and compliance. Key use cases include automating routine security tasks (46%), improving SOC alert triage (42%), and enhancing risk assessment and threat modeling (35%). This widespread adoption of AI for security purposes, including faster correlation of adversarial threats and easier configuration of security controls, presents a strong upside driver for cybersecurity firms developing and deploying AI-powered defense solutions.
forces.source_title: Secure in India 2026: Cyber GCCs in the age of AI

forces.title: AI security challenges drive demand for new governance, risk solutions.
forces.description: The adoption of AI introduces significant security challenges for cyber GCCs, including data security and privacy, governance, regulatory and compliance risks, as well as model and system vulnerabilities. These concerns compel organizations to implement new AI security management activities, such as AI security policies and standards (47%), the establishment of AI regulatory and governance functions (35%), and dedicated AI risk assessment frameworks (31%). This rapidly evolving risk landscape acts as a key risk, simultaneously creating demand for specialized cybersecurity products and services focused on AI governance and risk management.
forces.source_title: Secure in India 2026: Cyber GCCs in the age of AI

forces.title: Cyber GCCs boost innovation and R&D in critical security domains.
forces.description: Cyber Global Capability Centers (GCCs) are significantly increasing their R&D and innovation efforts, with 65% now having cybersecurity labs and 67% increasing investment since 2023. Key innovation domains include cybersecurity operations, risk assessments, engineering, and IAM. This focus is driven by a future demand for specialized expertise (23%) and widespread adoption of autonomous cybersecurity operations (21%). The establishment of Centres of Excellence (COEs) in incident response, threat management, AI security, third-party security, and cloud security further strengthens India's cybersecurity capabilities and offerings.
forces.source_title: Secure in India 2026: Cyber GCCs in the age of AI

forces.title: Evolving regulatory landscape and third-party risk challenge cyber leadership.
forces.description: Cyber Global Capability Center (GCC) leadership faces significant cybersecurity challenges, including navigating a rapidly changing regulatory landscape (13% citing it as a top challenge) and effectively managing third-party cybersecurity risk (11%). The rise of emerging cybersecurity attacks, particularly those driven by new technologies, further complicates the environment (9%). These challenges, alongside the need to embed a strong risk culture, necessitate continuous adaptation of cybersecurity strategies and investments in advanced risk management and compliance solutions.
forces.source_title: Secure in India 2026: Cyber GCCs in the age of AI

forces.title: Cloud adoption challenges misconfiguration, regulatory complexity for cyber.
forces.description: Cyber Global Capability Centers (GCCs) encounter significant cybersecurity challenges during cloud adoption, primarily misconfiguration and inadequate change control (15% of challenges). Regulatory compliance in cloud environments (13%) and the requirement for multiple cloud security tools for comprehensive "code to cloud" security (10%) also pose substantial hurdles. These challenges highlight the need for robust cloud security posture management (CSPM), compliance automation, and integrated security platforms to mitigate risks associated with multi-cloud deployments.
forces.source_title: Secure in India 2026: Cyber GCCs in the age of AI

forces.title: AI security threats elevate global board-level cybersecurity risks.
forces.description: Global boards are increasingly tracking AI misuse as a top cybersecurity risk, alongside OT security risk, software supply chain security risk, and third-party security risk. While critical infrastructure, cloud expansion, and regulatory risks remain prominent, the emergence of AI as a significant threat vector reflects a growing concern at the highest levels of governance. This necessitates focused investment in AI security solutions and robust risk management frameworks to address the evolving nature of threats originating from or amplified by artificial intelligence.
forces.source_title: Secure in India 2026: Cyber GCCs in the age of AI

forces.title: Cyber fusion centers enhance incident response and threat intelligence.
forces.description: Cyber Global Capability Centers (GCCs) have significantly scaled up cyber fusion centers and dedicated cybersecurity Centres of Excellence (COEs), complementing their expanded Security Operation Centers (SOCs). Key benefits realized include faster incident response times (21%), improved threat intelligence sharing (21%), and better overall cybersecurity outcomes (21%). This strategic investment in integrated security operations platforms and expertise acts as a strong upside driver, enabling organizations to proactively detect, analyze, and respond to sophisticated cyber threats more efficiently.
forces.source_title: Secure in India 2026: Cyber GCCs in the age of AI

forces.title: Rapid expansion of cyber GCCs boosts India's cybersecurity sector.
forces.description: India has seen exponential growth in cybersecurity functions within Global Capability Centers (GCCs), with 61% establishing their cyber presence in the last decade. Post-2023 GCCs inherently incorporate cybersecurity, while older ones significantly expanded their functions between 2023-2026. This trend has led to over 25% of cyber GCCs hosting nearly half their global cybersecurity workforce in India, with 23% having 100-200 members. This concentration of talent and activity serves as a powerful tailwind for the growth and development of India's cybersecurity sector.
forces.source_title: Secure in India 2026: Cyber GCCs in the age of AI

forces.title: India's cyber GCC leadership gains global influence in security.
forces.description: The leadership in India's cyber Global Capability Centers (GCCs) is gaining significant global influence, with 51% of organizations reporting global teams directly to India-based cyber GCC leaders. This indicates increased maturity in delivering cybersecurity and digital risk management services worldwide. Furthermore, 98% of cyber GCCs in India consistently adopt the Three Lines of Defence (3LOD) model for cybersecurity risk management across all sectors, establishing a standardized and robust approach that structurally elevates India's role in global cybersecurity governance.
forces.source_title: Secure in India 2026: Cyber GCCs in the age of AI

forces.title: Integrated cybersecurity activities drive risk reduction across 3LOD in GCCs.
forces.description: Cyber Global Capability Centers (GCCs) are undertaking a wide range of integrated cybersecurity activities across the Three Lines of Defence (3LOD) model. This includes foundational areas like Application/Infrastructure Security and Cloud Security (LOD1), strategic functions like Cybersecurity Risk Assessments and Third-Party Risk Management (LOD2), and assurance activities such as Cybersecurity Audits (LOD3). This comprehensive approach, exemplified by a financial services GCC conducting global risk-based internal audits, structurally improves risk reduction, enhances governance of emerging technologies like AI, and strengthens confidence in business-critical platforms.
forces.source_title: Secure in India 2026: Cyber GCCs in the age of AI

forces.title: Skilled cybersecurity talent in India drives cyber GCC growth.
forces.description: The availability of skilled cybersecurity resources in India continues to be the primary driver for leveraging the Global Capability Center (GCC) model, significantly boosting the sector's growth. This is complemented by the GCCs' ability to provide uninterrupted service delivery and foster continuous innovation and agility. The expansion of core cybersecurity functions delivered from India, now including specialized areas like AI security, OT security, and Quantum security, further solidifies India's role as a critical talent and service provider for global cybersecurity operations.
forces.source_title: Secure in India 2026: Cyber GCCs in the age of AI

forces.title: Cybersecurity budgets shift towards operations, cloud, data, AI.
forces.description: Budget allocations for cybersecurity functions are undergoing a structural shift, with cybersecurity operations, cloud security, data security & privacy, incident response & management, and Identity and Access Management (IAM) emerging as the top five priorities in 2026. This indicates a heightened focus on core defensive capabilities and securing modern IT environments. Additionally, emerging technology risk, cyber resilience, and AI security are gaining prominence, signaling a move towards proactive and integrated security strategies that will continue to drive spending in these specialized areas.
forces.source_title: Secure in India 2026: Cyber GCCs in the age of AI

forces.title: Escalating cyberattacks drive demand for cost-effective GCC cybersecurity.
forces.description: The continuous increase in the intensity and scope of cybersecurity attacks, coupled with limited budget growth for cybersecurity functions in global organizations, is a primary catalyst for cyber Global Capability Center (GCC) growth. GCCs offer significant value by providing cost arbitrage, high competency, and agility in cybersecurity operations. This dynamic positions India's cyber GCCs as crucial strategic partners, as global enterprises increasingly rely on them to manage expanding cyber threats efficiently and effectively, boosting the demand for their services.
forces.source_title: Secure in India 2026: Cyber GCCs in the age of AI

forces.title: IAM, data, and cloud security drive significant increases in cyber spending.
forces.description: Cybersecurity spending is heavily increasing across core IN080203 categories. Identity and Access Management (IAM) leads with 69% of organizations increasing spend, followed by Data Security and Privacy (65%) and Cloud Security Posture Management (60%). Other significant increases are seen in SOC Optimization (58%), Cloud Workload and Container Protection (41%), and Managed Detection and Response (35%). This widespread investment reflects the critical importance of these domains in modern defense strategies and acts as a strong tailwind for the growth of cybersecurity providers.
forces.source_title: Cybersecurity Budgets Are Growing Fast. AI Threats Are Growing Faster.

forces.title: AI simultaneously expands attack surface and enhances cyber defenses.
forces.description: Artificial Intelligence (AI) is fundamentally reshaping the cybersecurity landscape by simultaneously creating new cyber and data privacy risks, thus significantly expanding the digital attack surface. Concurrently, AI has become a potent tool in the hacker's arsenal, enabling faster, more scalable, and frequent attacks. In response, organizations are rapidly adopting AI-powered cybersecurity capabilities to counter these evolving threats. This dual impact of AI represents a profound structural change, driving both an increased threat level and the necessary evolution of defensive technologies within the cybersecurity industry.
forces.source_title: Cybersecurity Budgets Are Growing Fast. AI Threats Are Growing Faster.

forces.title: AI-enabled attacks inflict significant operational and financial impact.
forces.description: The BCG & GLG CISO Survey 4.0 reveals that a substantial portion of companies (roughly one-third) experienced significant operational or financial impact from AI-enabled cyberattacks in the last 12 months, with 35% reporting such severe consequences from at least one threat. This includes AI-driven targeted social engineering, AI-powered malware, and AI-enabled fraud schemes. This high impact underscores the critical and immediate threat posed by malicious AI use, necessitating urgent and robust investment in advanced defensive cybersecurity solutions and strategies.
forces.source_title: Cybersecurity Budgets Are Growing Fast. AI Threats Are Growing Faster.

forces.title: Cyber incumbents, hyperscalers, and startups dominate AI security tools market.
forces.description: The market for AI-powered cybersecurity tools is fragmented and dynamic, with "cyber platform incumbents" (e.g., Palo Alto Networks, Crowdstrike, Microsoft) being adopted by 64% of organizations primarily as complements to existing security tools. Hyperscaler solutions (e.g., AWS, Azure, GCP) are favored by 63% for their ease of integration, while "AI-enabled security startups" (e.g., Abnormal AI, Darktrace) capture 39% of the market in niche domains. This competitive landscape reflects a structural shift in how AI security solutions are sourced and integrated across enterprises.
forces.source_title: Cybersecurity Budgets Are Growing Fast. AI Threats Are Growing Faster.

forces.title: Cyber maturity drives divergent strategies in tool consolidation.
forces.description: Organizations' cybersecurity maturity levels dictate their approach to tool consolidation. Advanced organizations prioritize tighter integration for a "single pane of glass" view and cross-domain visibility (32%), aiming to reduce complexity. Conversely, less mature ("emerging") organizations are more driven by the need to reduce cost (33%) and achieve better standalone product capabilities with vendors of choice (27%). This divergence represents a structural change in vendor selection and solution architecture within the cybersecurity market, with mature players seeking platform approaches and others focusing on point solutions for specific gaps.
forces.source_title: Cybersecurity Budgets Are Growing Fast. AI Threats Are Growing Faster.

forces.title: Agentic AI introduces new risks, emphasizes human-in-the-loop cyber defense.
forces.description: The emergence of "agentic AI" in cybersecurity introduces new risks and necessitates robust guardrails and human-in-the-loop decision-making. This structural change means that while AI can enhance defenses across the cybersecurity lifecycle (governance, identification, protection, detection, response, recovery), its autonomous nature requires disciplined deployment. Organizations must strategically integrate AI, acknowledging its capacity to create and mitigate threats, thereby fundamentally altering the operational model for cybersecurity teams and requiring new governance mechanisms.
forces.source_title: Empowering defenders: AI for cybersecurity

forces.title: Tier-II/III cities attract cybersecurity talent with cost savings.
forces.description: Non-metro cities in India are experiencing a structural shift in IT hiring, with over 50% growth in H1 2025, significantly outperforming traditional hubs like Bengaluru. These tier-II and tier-III cities are increasingly attracting demand for talent in AI, cloud, and cybersecurity, offering approximately 30% cost savings. This trend creates a new geographic distribution for cybersecurity talent and operations, enabling companies to expand their workforce more affordably while potentially tapping into diverse skill pools outside major metropolitan areas.
forces.source_title: Information Technology And BPM Industry In India

forces.title: GCCs to drive substantial new tech job creation, including cybersecurity.
forces.description: Global Capability Centers (GCCs) in India are projected to generate 22-25% of all net new white-collar tech jobs in 2025. Of the 4.7 million new tech jobs anticipated by 2027, over 1.2 million are expected from GCCs, primarily driven by advancements in Generative AI and engineering R&D. This massive influx of talent will significantly benefit the cybersecurity sector within GCCs, ensuring a robust talent pipeline for specialized roles and acting as a strong tailwind for the industry's growth and capacity.
forces.source_title: Information Technology And BPM Industry In India

forces.title: M&A activity in India's tech sector targets cybersecurity capabilities.
forces.description: India's tech sector is experiencing a surge in M&A activity, with firms actively seeking niche skills. A notable acquisition includes Infosys buying cybersecurity firm The Missing Link. This trend, part of broader investment to expand capabilities in cloud, AI, cyber, and chip design, acts as an upside driver for the cybersecurity sector. It indicates consolidation and strategic investment by larger players to enhance their cybersecurity offerings and expand market presence, potentially valuing specialized cybersecurity firms at a premium.
forces.source_title: Information Technology And BPM Industry In India

forces.title: Government strengthens cybersecurity framework, invests in infrastructure protection.
forces.description: The Indian government has significantly bolstered its cybersecurity framework through initiatives like CERT-In, NCIIPC, NCCC, and the Digital Personal Data Protection Act, 2023. These efforts include widespread security drills and training for officials to combat rising cyber threats. A budget allocation of Rs. 782 crore (US$ 88.90 million) in 2025–26 specifically targets cybersecurity measures for digital public infrastructure. This proactive stance represents a structural change, creating a more secure operating environment and driving demand for advanced cybersecurity products and services.
forces.source_title: Information Technology And BPM Industry In India

forces.title: Doubling of cyber incidents indicates escalating threat landscape in India.
forces.description: Cyber incidents handled by CERT-In have doubled in India over the last four years, indicating a significant and rapidly escalating threat landscape. This includes major breaches like cloud misconfiguration exposing client data at top retail brokers, ransomware attacks freezing 300 banks via a shared tech vendor, and sophisticated heists on crypto exchanges. This trend poses a critical risk to the overall digital economy, particularly for mid-tier BFSI entities that are highly digitized and interconnected but possess fractional cybersecurity budgets compared to larger players, driving urgent demand for enhanced defenses.
forces.source_title: Cybersecurity in the Age of AI

forces.title: Supply chain and third-party risks escalate for Indian BFSI.
forces.description: Supply chain risk and third-party dependencies have become a growing and critical priority for the Indian BFSI sector. Sophisticated financial players' increasing reliance on external FTEs, outsourced cloud, and data storage services, coupled with AI amplifying vulnerabilities, elevates this risk. A single incident in July 2024, where a shared-vendor breach impacted 300 banks, demonstrates the acute concentration risk. With 55% of Indian BFSI CXOs prioritizing this, it drives urgent demand for enhanced third-party risk management and continuous monitoring solutions.
forces.source_title: Cybersecurity in the Age of AI

forces.title: AI widens critical cybersecurity advanced skills gap in India.
forces.description: Cybersecurity talent is identified as a critical constraint in India, with the rapid advancement of Artificial Intelligence (AI) further widening the advanced skills gap. This challenge means that while demand for cybersecurity professionals is soaring due to escalating AI-enabled threats, the availability of adequately skilled personnel, particularly in specialized AI security, is lagging. This persistent talent deficit poses a significant key risk to organizations' ability to effectively implement and manage sophisticated cybersecurity defenses, potentially slowing down adoption of new security technologies.
forces.source_title: Cybersecurity in the Age of AI

forces.title: Data protection maturity high, third-party risk lags in Indian BFSI.
forces.description: In Indian BFSI, data protection is a highly mature cybersecurity capability, with 79% of firms operating at active or continuous maturity stages, likely due to long-standing regulatory pressure. However, third-party and supply chain risk management significantly lags, with only 49% of firms achieving mature practice. This disparity creates a structural gap, as the pace of threat evolution outpaces existing controls in a sector with extensive third-party exposure, posing a critical key risk for overall cybersecurity resilience despite strong data protection.
forces.source_title: Cybersecurity in the Age of AI

forces.title: AI-enabled social engineering and identity attacks dominate BFSI threat agenda.
forces.description: AI-driven threats, particularly deepfake social engineering and Generative AI (GenAI) data leakage, have structurally shifted the Indian BFSI threat agenda, becoming present defensive priorities. Traditional concerns like denial-of-service attacks have diminished in prominence (down to 17%), displaced by these more sophisticated and personalized AI-enabled attacks. This change necessitates a strong focus on identity-centric security, advanced threat detection for AI-generated content, and data loss prevention specifically tailored to mitigate these evolving attack vectors, driving investment in relevant IN080203 solutions.
forces.source_title: Cybersecurity in the Age of AI

forces.title: Indian BFSI struggles with third-party code dependency visibility for vulnerabilities.
forces.description: While Indian BFSI shows confidence in compensating controls for unpatchable vulnerabilities (62%), a significant weakness lies in its ability to identify dependencies on third-party code, with only 45% confidence in knowing actual system components. This blind spot severely impairs the sector's capacity to anticipate and respond to disclosures of high-severity vulnerabilities, particularly those identified through frontier AI capabilities. This key risk exposes organizations to unanticipated threats originating from their complex software supply chains, driving demand for software supply chain security and enhanced visibility tools.
forces.source_title: Cybersecurity in the Age of AI

forces.title: Shift to risk-based cyber budgeting reorients security investment.
forces.description: A proposed structural change in cybersecurity budgeting calls for a shift from traditional line-item categories like endpoint or network security to risk-based categories such as "ransomware disruption risk" or "third-party access exposure." This reorientation forces every budget item to be justified by its ability to reduce quantified risk, rather than inertia. This move requires greater collaboration across security, finance, and enterprise risk functions, aiming for budgets that are adaptive, transparent, and more closely aligned with business outcomes.
forces.source_title: A risk-based approach to cyber budgets

forces.title: Cyber risk quantification (CRQ) becomes essential for justifying security spend.
forces.description: The shift towards risk-driven budgeting in cybersecurity necessitates the eventual requirement for cyber risk quantification (CRQ). Frameworks like FAIR (Factor Analysis of Information Risk) will be crucial for assigning financial values to risks such as ransomware, insider misuse, third-party dependencies, and AI misuse. This structural change aims to enable CISOs to demonstrate efficiency and effectiveness by articulating security investments in terms of "risk reduction per dollar spent," transforming how security initiatives are proposed, justified, and approved by senior leadership.
forces.source_title: A risk-based approach to cyber budgets

forces.title: Agentic AI and digital agents intensify digital identity management scrutiny.
forces.description: The proliferation of agentic AI and digital agents fundamentally reshapes the landscape of digital identity management. CISOs face increased scrutiny and complexity in protecting the vast number of non-human identities. These autonomous agents, capable of creating and deleting other agents, demand new approaches to identity governance, access controls, and continuous monitoring. This structural change in identity management requirements will drive significant investment in advanced IAM solutions and specialized security services to cope with the challenges introduced by AI-driven automation.
forces.source_title: Cybersecurity considerations 2026

forces.title: Quantum computing poses existential threat, drives PQC transition.
forces.description: Quantum computing presents a significant, medium-term threat, necessitating a crucial transition to post-quantum cryptography (PQC). This transformation is deemed an "existential one" for critical sectors like finance and defense, requiring proactive preparation to maintain resilience and business continuity. The impending capability of quantum computers to break current encryption standards drives urgent demand for PQC solutions and expertise, representing a structural shift in cryptographic security and a high-impact risk for any organization relying on strong encryption.
forces.source_title: Cybersecurity considerations 2026

forces.title: IT/OT hyperconnectivity and IoT increase critical infrastructure vulnerability.
forces.description: The increasing hyperconnectivity between IT and Operational Technology (OT) environments, especially with the proliferation of IoT devices, significantly raises the vulnerability of critical infrastructure in sectors like Utilities, Oil & Gas, and Manufacturing. Data centers themselves are now recognized as critical infrastructure, escalating the need to safeguard associated power and utility facilities, particularly those with obsolete legacy technology. This structural trend represents a high-impact key risk, driving demand for specialized OT security solutions, cyber-physical protection, and enhanced monitoring capabilities to manage the expanded attack surface.
forces.source_title: Cybersecurity considerations 2026

forces.title: Cybersecurity and digital risk resilience become top CEO investment priority.
forces.description: Cybersecurity has become an enterprise-wide priority, with the KPMG 2025 CEO Outlook identifying "cybersecurity and digital risk resilience" as one of the top pressures influencing investment decisions. This signifies a structural shift where security is no longer solely an IT concern but a core business enabler and a differentiator. This executive-level focus drives increased budget allocation and strategic integration of cybersecurity measures across all business functions, aiming to build stakeholder trust, reduce capital costs, and facilitate new product development in a competitive market.
forces.source_title: Cybersecurity considerations 2026

forces.title: RBI advisory strengthens customer data protection requirements for SEs.
forces.description: An RBI advisory based on a 2025 thematic study outlines leading practices for customer data protection and management for Supervised Entities (SEs). This includes mandates for clear governance structures, strong security controls (especially cloud security), defined data retention/destruction, robust complaint mechanisms, and comprehensive incident response frameworks with 24x7 monitoring and layered security controls like EDR. This guidance acts as a structural change, demanding higher standards for data security and privacy, and driving increased adoption of advanced cybersecurity solutions across financial services.
forces.source_title: RBI advisory on customer data protection and management

forces.title: AI-driven fraud detection requires robust governance, continuous monitoring.
forces.description: In financial services, AI-driven fraud detection, while highly accurate, introduces new challenges related to transparency, data privacy, and potential biases. This structural change demands that organizations embed security into design, reinforce governance, and maintain human oversight, including continuous monitoring of AI systems. This drives demand for specialized cybersecurity solutions that can audit, secure, and ensure the ethical deployment of AI within critical financial applications, balancing innovation with stringent risk management and compliance.
forces.source_title: Cybersecurity considerations 2026

forces.title: Geopolitics and cyber activity expose defense supply chains.
forces.description: Political fragmentation and persistent grey-zone cyber activity are significantly exposing defense supply chains to continuous compromise, particularly across software, Operational Technology (OT), and critical infrastructure. This poses a high-impact key risk to operational resilience and mission assurance. In response, defense organizations are prioritizing continuous supply chain detection and response mechanisms, driving increased demand for integrated security solutions that provide deep visibility and rapid response capabilities across complex and often geographically dispersed supply chain ecosystems.
forces.source_title: Cybersecurity considerations 2026

forces.title: RBI mandates governance, monitoring, risk mitigation for AI/ML in financial services.
forces.description: The RBI's advisory on customer data protection mandates the establishment of explicit governance, monitoring, and risk mitigation mechanisms for the utilization of AI/Machine Learning (ML) and equivalent technologies in financial services. This requirement, under "Emerging technologies and data risks," compels Supervised Entities to implement SIEM platforms, real-time API monitoring, anomaly detection, and regular penetration testing. This structural change significantly increases the compliance burden and drives demand for specialized cybersecurity solutions that can secure and govern AI/ML deployments in sensitive financial contexts.
forces.source_title: RBI advisory on customer data protection and management

forces.title: Autonomous security and AI-SPM reshape SOC and identity management.
forces.description: The rise of autonomous security, with agents performing intelligence-driven tasks in the SOC, compliance, risk, and identity management, represents a fundamental structural change. This is driven by the proliferation of non-human identities and "shadow agents," which necessitate a centralized identity store, policy-based access controls, and a new "AI security posture management (AI-SPM)." CISOs are compelled to integrate autonomous security architectures into their SOCs, supported by continuous monitoring and improvement of AI models, data, and infrastructure, to manage the high volume of AI-generated events and evolving threats.
forces.source_title: Cybersecurity considerations 2026

viewpoints.title: India's Cyber GCCs redefine global cybersecurity and risk management in AI era.
viewpoints.description: KPMG asserts that Cyber Global Capability Centers (GCCs) in India have evolved beyond support roles to become strategic leaders in cybersecurity and digital risk management. Amid a landscape of intense cyber-warfare, sophisticated attacks, and AI-induced risks, these GCCs are driving innovation, building resilience, and contributing significantly to business growth for their global organizations. Their expanding ecosystem and focus on future-ready talent underscore India's pivotal role in global cybersecurity leadership.
viewpoints.source_title: Secure in India 2026: Cyber GCCs in the age of AI

viewpoints.title: India poised as global hub for cyber resilience and business transformation.
viewpoints.description: Vinayak Godse, CEO of DSCI, states that India is uniquely positioned to become a global hub for business transformation and cyber resilience leadership. This is driven by its deep talent pool, vibrant innovation ecosystem, and growing cybersecurity capabilities. As GCCs in India take on greater strategic responsibilities, their cybersecurity maturity, investment in advanced threat detection, cloud security, AI-enabled operations, and identity-centric architectures are becoming critical differentiators, reinforcing the nation's leadership in securing digital operations globally.
viewpoints.source_title: Secure in India 2026: Cyber GCCs in the age of AI

viewpoints.title: India's IT industry poised to lead global cybersecurity talent development.
viewpoints.description: KPMG highlights India's potential to address the global cybersecurity talent shortage, a challenge exacerbated by the weaponization of cybersecurity and AI-driven attacks. Citing Prime Minister Modi's 2015 call to action, the report suggests India's Global Capability Centers (GCCs) are strategically positioned to provide specialized cybersecurity skills that the global talent pool currently lacks. This focus on building and scaling expertise within India's GCC ecosystem offers a reliable outcome for global organizations dealing with business disruption and rapid cloud/AI adoption.
viewpoints.source_title: Secure in India 2026: Cyber GCCs in the age of AI

viewpoints.title: India's robust cybersecurity ecosystem provides global competitive advantage.
viewpoints.description: Dr. Sanjay Bahl, DG of CERT-In, posits that India's journey in cybersecurity has created a compelling success story, building a world-class workforce and a sustainable ecosystem. This includes fostering innovation, developing indigenous capabilities, and scaling 'Make in India' cybersecurity products. Cyber GCCs are now a strategic component, acting as a source of competitive advantage for global organizations seeking resilience and growth. The opportunity lies in combining India's talent, innovation, and scale to build a more secure, resilient, and trusted digital future.
viewpoints.source_title: Secure in India 2026: Cyber GCCs in the age of AI

viewpoints.title: AI adoption to drive sustained acceleration in cybersecurity spending growth.
viewpoints.description: According to a BCG & GLG CISO Survey, nearly half (49%) of CISOs anticipate that the adoption of AI will lead to a sustained acceleration in cybersecurity spend growth. This outlook suggests that the initial increases in budgets driven by AI-related threats and defenses are not temporary, but rather represent a long-term trend. The expectation is that AI's continuous evolution will necessitate ongoing and expanding investments in cybersecurity solutions to keep pace with both new risks and enhanced defensive capabilities.
viewpoints.source_title: Cybersecurity Budgets Are Growing Fast. AI Threats Are Growing Faster.

viewpoints.title: AI is powerful force for modern cyber defense, requiring strategic deployment.
viewpoints.description: KPMG, in collaboration with the World Economic Forum, asserts that AI is a transformative power in cybersecurity, enabling organizations to strengthen resilience against AI-amplified attacks. While threat actors leverage AI for speed and sophistication, defenders can harness it for detection and response. The report emphasizes that successful AI integration in cybersecurity transcends mere automation, requiring strategic investments in technology, skills, and processes, coupled with rigorously tested use cases, strong governance, and human oversight from the outset for effective deployment.

viewpoints.title: India's BFSI sector faces significant cyber attack intensity challenges.
viewpoints.description: BCG highlights that the Indian Banking, Financial Services, and Insurance (BFSI) sector confronts a steep challenge in managing the intensity of cyberattacks. This assessment is based on various reports including Check Point Cyber Security Report, IBM Cost of a Data Breach Report, and BCG's CISO surveys. The sector's susceptibility to sophisticated threats, coupled with its critical role, implies an ongoing and elevated risk environment, necessitating continuous and robust investment in advanced cybersecurity solutions and resilient frameworks.
viewpoints.source_title: Cybersecurity in the Age of AI

viewpoints.title: Indian BFSI lacks confidence in AI-enabled cyber incident readiness.
viewpoints.description: A BCG x DSCI India CISO Survey 2026 reveals limited confidence among Indian BFSI leaders regarding their readiness for AI-enabled cyber incidents. For example, only 29% are highly confident in "Sandbox, container, and privilege boundary integrity," and 34% in "Non-human identity controls." This indicates that existing cyber defenses, built for human-paced threats, are largely untested against AI adversaries. The lack of quantification for Recovery Time Objective (RTO), Recovery Point Objective (RPO), and blast radius for AI-enabled incidents further underscores a critical preparedness gap.
viewpoints.source_title: Cybersecurity in the Age of AI

viewpoints.title: CISOs concerned about AI attacks, yet underfund related cyber budgets.
viewpoints.description: BCG reports that 76% of CISOs rank AI-enabled attacks among their top four concerns, underscoring the severity of this evolving threat. However, a significant gap exists between concern and investment, as only 19% of CISOs have increased their cyber budgets by more than 10% to address these specific threats. This suggests a potential underfunding of critical defense mechanisms against AI-driven risks, highlighting a disparity that could leave organizations vulnerable despite high awareness of the problem.
viewpoints.source_title: Cybersecurity in the Age of AI

viewpoints.title: Indian BFSI CISOs highly concerned about rapid AI-based cyberattacks.
viewpoints.description: According to a BCG x DSCI India CISO Survey, 69% of Indian BFSI CISOs express "very" or "extremely" high concern about AI-based cyberattacks in the next 12 months. This reflects a dramatic increase in attack pace, from traditional multi-day reconnaissance to immediate exploitation, and a significant growth in sophistication due to AI-generated attack paths, as highlighted by industry CISOs. This profound apprehension signals an urgent need for advanced, AI-aware defensive strategies and solutions within the financial sector.
viewpoints.source_title: Cybersecurity in the Age of AI

viewpoints.title: Cyber budgets need risk-based alignment for effective investment.
viewpoints.description: KPMG asserts that cybersecurity budgets are often misaligned with actual organizational risk, leading to inefficient resource allocation. The firm advocates for a principles-based framework: alignment of every budget category to a quantified risk, adaptability to evolving threats, and transparency linking spending to measurable risk reduction. This approach necessitates shifting budget categories from technical domains (e.g., endpoint security) to risk categories (e.g., ransomware disruption risk), ensuring investments are justified by quantifiable business outcomes and foster greater resilience.
viewpoints.source_title: A risk-based approach to cyber budgets

viewpoints.title: AI is double-edged sword, intensifying cyber risks and defense opportunities.
viewpoints.description: KPMG states that AI presents a dual challenge and opportunity for cybersecurity professionals. While AI empowers threat actors with faster, more sophisticated attacks, it also offers defenders a potent tool to detect and address threats more efficiently than humans alone. The proliferation of agentic AI and digital agents adds complexity, intensifying scrutiny on digital identity management, particularly for non-human identities. This dynamic environment necessitates that CISOs strategically leverage AI while navigating evolving geopolitical landscapes and regulatory complexities to maintain trusted operations.

demand_drivers.description: The RBI's new technology-focused master directions for cybersecurity and digital payments security necessitate gap assessments, remediation planning, and continuous compliance efforts across regulated entities. This drives demand for consulting, implementation, and managed services related to technology governance, cybersecurity, operational resilience, and assurance.

new_opportunities.description: The complexity and immediate effectiveness of RBI's consolidated cybersecurity and digital payments security directions create significant opportunities for cybersecurity firms to offer specialized advisory, gap assessment, remediation planning, and ongoing operational support services to regulated entities in India.

market_sizing.methodology: Discussion of the compliance requirements driving demand for cybersecurity services related to RBI's new directions.
market_sizing.source_title: RBI’s technology focused master directions issued on 31 July 2026

demand_drivers.description: Increased cybersecurity spending is largely driven by the adoption of Artificial Intelligence, which simultaneously creates new risks and enables new defensive capabilities, necessitating higher investment in security infrastructure and tools.

pnl_drivers.description: Cybersecurity budgets continue to outpace projections, with 2026 survey respondents forecasting a 14% increase in spending for the coming year, indicating a growing willingness to invest in protection.

market_sizing.methodology: Global CISO survey data on year-over-year cybersecurity spend growth projections.
market_sizing.source_title: Cybersecurity Budgets Are Growing Fast. AI Threats Are Growing Faster.

demand_drivers.description: The Indian government's allocation of funds for cybersecurity is driven by the imperative to protect critical digital public infrastructure, combat rising cyber threats, and strengthen the overall national cybersecurity framework.

market_sizing.methodology: Government budget allocation for cybersecurity measures to protect digital public infrastructure.
